name: EBCI Blue Corn Tortillas
region: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians / Indigenous Americas
imageAlt: Illustrative blue corn tortillas; this photograph was taken in Baja California and is not presented as an EBCI-specific tortilla photograph
imageCredit: Photo: T.Tseng, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY 2.0. The image illustrates blue corn tortillas generally and is not presented as an Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians-specific photograph.
summary: Blue corn tortillas adapted from a recipe by chef and food historian Lois Ellen Frank and published by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods program.
lead: Blue corn masa meets a hot cast-iron skillet in a modern EBCI-published recipe that also teaches why nixtamalization matters.
about: The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods program publishes this Blue Corn Tortillas recipe by chef and food historian Lois Ellen Frank. It combines white masa harina with finely ground blue cornmeal and explains the role of nixtamalization—the alkaline treatment that transforms corn into hominy or masa and improves flavor, workability and nutrition.
story: This is best understood as a contemporary Indigenous community recipe rather than an attempt to claim that the Mexican-style pressed tortilla is an ancient Cherokee form. EBCI Tribal Foods chose to publish the recipe within its living foodways collection, and Frank uses it to teach a much older Indigenous technology: nixtamalization. That distinction matters because Indigenous foodways continue to adapt while preserving knowledge about corn.
caveat: This page follows a modern recipe publicly published by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and credited to Lois Ellen Frank. The hero photograph shows blue corn tortillas photographed in Mexico and is used only as a visual example of the finished tortilla form.
prepNotes: Use masa harina, not plain cornmeal
Nixtamalized masa harina supplies the binding structure; blue cornmeal alone will crumble.
Judge dough by touch
A pressed edge should stay smooth instead of cracking badly; add warm water a teaspoon at a time if dry.
Keep cooked tortillas wrapped
Stacking in a towel lets steam soften them after the skillet.
ingredients: 1/2 cup finely ground blue corn flour or blue cornmeal
steps: Whisk masa harina, blue corn flour, salt and baking powder in a bowl.
Add most of the warm water and mix with your hands until a soft cohesive dough forms. Rest 5 minutes.
Checkpoint: squeeze a small ball and flatten it. If the edge splits deeply, knead in water 1 teaspoon at a time; if sticky, add a spoonful of masa harina.
Divide into 10 balls slightly smaller than golf balls. Heat a seasoned cast-iron skillet or comal over medium-high heat.
Press each ball between plastic sheets in a tortilla press to about 5 inches across.
Peel away the plastic carefully and cook on the dry hot skillet about 60–90 seconds on the first side, flip, then cook another 60–90 seconds.
Checkpoint: the tortilla should show toasted brown spots and may puff in places while remaining flexible rather than crisp.
Stack finished tortillas inside a clean towel or covered basket and serve warm.
sources: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Blue Corn Tortillas by Lois Ellen Frank

name: Ethiopian Genfo
imageAlt: Genfo or ga'at porridge from northern Ethiopia with a seasoned butter well in the center
imageCredit: Photo: UMarooB, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Ethiopian genfo: a very thick wheat porridge shaped into a mound with a central well of niter kibbeh and berbere for dipping each bite.
lead: Flour and water become a dense, smooth breakfast porridge built around the brilliant red pool of spiced butter at its center.
about: Genfo is a thick Ethiopian porridge prepared from cereal flour and water. Wheat, barley, maize and other grains are used depending on household and region. The cooked porridge is shaped in a bowl and a well is made in the center for niter kibbeh mixed with berbere; diners pull pieces from the outer mound and dip them into the seasoned fat.
story: An Ethiopian Ministry of Labor and Skills training module describes genfo as a common breakfast made by stirring roasted cereal flour into boiling water until extremely thick and smooth, then filling a central well with clarified spiced butter and berbere. Published Ethiopian home recipes also associate genfo with nourishment for new mothers. The exact flour varies, which is why this accessible version uses wheat while acknowledging barley and maize traditions.
caveat: Regional names, grains and accompaniments differ, including ga'at in Tigrinya-speaking areas. Claims about postpartum health benefits should be understood as cultural practice rather than medical advice.
prepNotes: Use a sturdy spoon
The mixture becomes much thicker than oatmeal and requires force to fold smooth.
Add flour gradually
Dumping it all at once traps dry pockets that are difficult to remove.
Serve immediately
Genfo firms dramatically as it cools.
ingredients: 4 cups water, plus more as needed
steps: Whisk flour with cardamom if using. Bring water and salt to a strong boil in a heavy saucepan.
Reduce heat to medium-low and add the flour gradually while stirring vigorously with a sturdy wooden spoon.
Continue stirring, pressing and folding for 10–15 minutes. Add small splashes of hot water only if dry flour remains trapped.
Checkpoint: the porridge should become smooth, glossy and extremely thick enough to pull away from parts of the pan in one mass.
Transfer to a shallow bowl and smooth into a mound. Use the back of a cup or spoon to press a deep well into the center.
Melt niter kibbeh gently in a small pan and stir in berbere for about 30 seconds, just until fragrant.
Pour the red seasoned butter into the central well. Serve very hot, optionally with yogurt alongside, pulling spoonfuls of porridge through the spiced butter.
sources: Ethiopian Ministry of Labor and Skills — Preparing Ethiopian Cereal and Vegetable Dishes

name: Senegalese Mafé
imageCredit: Photo: Nicolas PHULPIN, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Senegalese mafé with a deep peanut-tomato sauce, beef and vegetables simmered until tender and served over rice.
lead: Peanuts become a savory sauce rather than a garnish in Senegalese mafé, carrying tomato, meat and vegetables into one rich stew.
about: Mafé is a West African peanut stew or sauce with especially strong associations in Senegal and Mali. Senegalese versions may contain meat, fish or vegetables and are generally served with rice. Peanut paste supplies both body and flavor, while tomato, onion and stock keep the sauce savory rather than dessert-like.
story: Senegalese chef Pierre Thiam describes mafé as an icon of Senegalese cuisine and one of West Africa’s foundational peanut sauces. He also connects Senegal’s enormous peanut production to colonial-era agricultural systems, showing how an ingredient can be both deeply embedded in contemporary cuisine and tied to a difficult economic history. This beef-and-vegetable version follows a familiar home-stew format while keeping the peanut sauce central.
caveat: Mafé exists across several West African countries with important local differences. This page is specifically framed as a Senegalese home version and does not claim that one peanut stew represents the entire region.
prepNotes: Use unsweetened peanut butter
Sugar and stabilizers can make the sauce cloying; natural peanut butter or ground peanut paste is best.
Whisk peanut butter with hot broth
Loosening it separately prevents stubborn lumps.
Add vegetables by cooking time
Root vegetables need longer than cabbage or okra.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb beef chuck, cut into 1-inch cubes
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Season beef lightly with salt. Heat oil in a Dutch oven and brown the beef in batches; transfer to a plate.
Add onion and cook 6–8 minutes until soft, then add garlic and tomato paste and cook 2 minutes.
Add crushed tomatoes and 4 cups stock. Return beef and simmer covered 30 minutes.
Whisk peanut butter with 1 cup hot broth from the pot until smooth, then stir the mixture back into the stew.
Add carrots, sweet potato and whole Scotch bonnet. Simmer 20 minutes.
Add cabbage and okra if using and continue 15–20 minutes.
Checkpoint: beef should be fork-tender, root vegetables soft but intact and the sauce thick enough to coat a spoon while still flowing over rice.
Remove the whole chile, season to taste and thin with remaining stock if needed. Serve over rice.
sources: Epicurious — Pierre Thiam on Senegalese Mafé
Epicurious — Pierre Thiam's Mafé Peanut Sauce

name: Trinidad Callaloo
imageAlt: Trinidadian callaloo, a thick leafy vegetable stew
imageCredit: Photo: GeoTrinity, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Trinidad callaloo with dasheen leaves, okra, pumpkin, coconut milk, aromatics and Scotch bonnet cooked down and swizzled into a thick green side dish.
lead: Dasheen leaves, okra and pumpkin melt into coconut milk until a whole Scotch bonnet has perfumed one of Trinidad’s defining Sunday-table dishes.
about: Trinidadian callaloo is a thick leafy dish made from dasheen or taro leaves with okra, pumpkin, coconut milk and aromatics. Crab or salted meat may be included, while meatless versions are also common. It is distinct from Jamaican sautéed callaloo greens and from other Caribbean dishes that share the same name.
story: Trinidad-raised food writer Brigid Washington describes callaloo as deeply rooted in Caribbean history and especially significant in Trinidad and Tobago. Foodie Nation’s Trinidadian method uses dasheen bush, okra, pumpkin, coconut milk, pimento peppers, herbs and a whole hot pepper, then partially purées the softened mixture. The goal is a thick, cohesive side dish rather than a thin soup.
caveat: Raw taro/dasheen leaves contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and must be cooked thoroughly. If true dasheen leaves are unavailable, collards plus spinach provide a practical but noticeably different substitute.
prepNotes: Cook dasheen completely
Do not taste raw or undercooked taro leaves; full cooking is essential.
Keep the Scotch bonnet intact
A whole unbroken chile adds aroma with more controlled heat.
Swizzle rather than liquefy
Traditional texture can retain some body instead of becoming a perfectly smooth purée.
ingredients: 1 lb cleaned dasheen/taro leaves, chopped, or 1 lb mixed collards and spinach
1 cup diced calabaza or butternut squash
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Heat oil in a large pot. Add onion, garlic and pimento peppers and cook 2–3 minutes until fragrant.
Add okra and pumpkin and sauté 4 minutes.
Add chopped dasheen leaves, thyme, culantro, coconut milk, water and the whole Scotch bonnet.
Bring to a simmer, cover and cook 25–30 minutes until every leaf and stem is completely tender and the pumpkin crushes easily.
Remove the Scotch bonnet intact. Checkpoint: there should be no raw firmness in the taro leaves and the okra and pumpkin should have naturally thickened the liquid.
Use a traditional swizzle stick, immersion blender or potato masher to break the mixture into a thick, somewhat textured stew rather than a completely smooth soup.
Stir in butter if using, season with salt and pepper and serve with rice, macaroni pie or Sunday lunch dishes.
sources: Foodie Nation — How to Make Trini Callaloo
Bon Appétit — Trini Callaloo by Trinidad-raised writer Brigid Washington
Food Network — Callaloo recipe courtesy of Asa Wright Nature Centre, Trinidad
Fringe Table — Caribbean & Lowcountry food guide

name: Sheki Piti
imageAlt: Azerbaijani piti served in its clay pot
imageCredit: Photo: Shahrux, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Sheki piti: lamb and chickpeas slow-cooked with saffron, chestnuts and dried sour fruit, traditionally served from individual clay pots in two stages.
lead: Lamb, chickpeas, saffron, chestnuts and sour fruit spend hours together in the clay pot before Sheki piti reaches the table twice: broth first, solids second.
about: Piti is a slow-cooked Azerbaijani lamb-and-chickpea dish especially associated with Sheki. Traditional Sheki versions are cooked in individual earthenware pots and may include lamb tail fat, chestnuts, dried plums and saffron. Serving is commonly a two-stage ritual: broth is poured over torn bread first, then the solids are mashed and eaten separately.
story: Azerbaijan’s official tourism material calls piti Sheki’s signature dish and describes it as a food still taught through local masterclasses and family traditions. Azerbaijani cuisine references specify lamb, chickpeas, tail fat, onion, chestnuts, dried plums and saffron for Sheki piti. The clay vessel and long, low cooking are not merely presentation—they create the soft chickpeas, yielding lamb and concentrated broth that define the dish.
caveat: Traditional cooks may simmer piti for much longer than a home oven schedule and use individual dopu clay pots. This adaptation uses small oven-safe clay pots or one Dutch oven while preserving the two-stage serving method.
prepNotes: Soak chickpeas overnight
They need a head start to become creamy during the slow cook.
Use a gentle oven
Hard boiling clouds the broth and can toughen meat.
Serve it twice
Broth over bread first and mashed solids second are part of the Sheki eating method.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups dried chickpeas, soaked overnight and drained
2 lb lamb shoulder, cut into 4 large portions
2 tbsp lamb fat or butter, optional
1/4 tsp saffron threads bloomed in 1/4 cup hot water
Lavash or crusty bread and sumac, for serving
steps: Heat oven to 325°F. Divide soaked chickpeas among four small oven-safe pots or place them in one heavy Dutch oven.
Nestle lamb over the chickpeas and add onion, chestnuts, dried plums and lamb fat if using.
Pour in saffron water and enough plain water to cover the solids comfortably. Season with salt.
Cover tightly and bake 2 1/2 hours, checking once and adding hot water if the chickpeas rise above the liquid.
Continue 20–40 minutes until lamb yields to a spoon and chickpeas are creamy inside.
Checkpoint: broth should be clear to lightly cloudy and intensely lamb-scented, with intact but fully tender chickpeas and soft fruit.
For the first course, ladle broth over torn bread and dust with sumac.
For the second course, spoon out the lamb, chickpeas, chestnuts and plums, mash lightly together and serve with more sumac and onion if desired.
sources: Azerbaijan Travel — Sheki cuisine and piti
Azerbaijans.com — Main dishes and Sheki pitisi ingredient specification

name: Sri Lankan Egg Hoppers (Bittara Appa)
imageAlt: Sri Lankan egg hoppers with crisp bowl-shaped edges and eggs in the centers
imageCredit: Photo: Dan arndt, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Sri Lankan egg hoppers made from fermented rice-flour and coconut batter swirled in a rounded pan until lacy at the edges, with an egg steamed in the center.
lead: Crisp as lace around the rim and tender in the bowl, a hopper becomes breakfast when an egg steams right in its center.
about: Hoppers, or appa, are bowl-shaped Sri Lankan pancakes made from fermented rice batter and coconut milk. The rounded hopper pan creates an exceptionally thin crisp rim while a small pool of batter stays soft in the center. For bittara appa, an egg is cracked into that center and cooks under a lid without flipping.
story: Sri Lanka Tourism lists hoppers among the island’s staple foods alongside string hoppers and pittu. They are eaten at breakfast and supper with sambols and curries, and egg hoppers are one of the most recognizable forms. Older methods can begin with soaked raw rice and a fermented starter; rice-flour-and-yeast batters are a common practical approach for modern kitchens.
caveat: Fermentation systems vary, including toddy, old batter and yeast. This home method uses yeast for predictability and should be understood as a practical adaptation rather than the only Sri Lankan hopper batter.
prepNotes: Use a rounded hopper pan if possible
The curved sides produce the crisp thin rim and soft center that a flat skillet cannot fully duplicate.
Ferment until bubbly
A batter with no visible aeration produces dense, leathery hoppers.
Serve immediately
Steam from the egg begins softening the crisp rim as soon as the hopper leaves the pan.
ingredients: 1 cup lukewarm water, plus more as needed
Neutral oil, for wiping the pan
Black pepper and salt, for the eggs
Pol sambol or lunu miris, for serving
steps: Whisk rice flour, yeast, sugar and 1 cup lukewarm water into a smooth thick batter. Cover and ferment in a warm place 3–4 hours until bubbly and lightly sour-smelling.
Whisk in coconut milk and salt. Add water gradually until the batter has the consistency of light cream and pours in a continuous stream.
Heat a hopper pan or small rounded wok over medium heat and wipe with a film of oil.
Pour in about 1/4 cup batter and immediately lift and swirl the pan so batter climbs the sides in a thin layer while a little remains pooled in the bottom.
Crack one egg into the center, season lightly, cover and cook 3–4 minutes.
Checkpoint: the edge should be deeply crisp and lacy, the center soft, the egg white opaque and the yolk cooked to your preference.
Run a thin spatula around the rim and lift the hopper out carefully. Repeat and serve each one immediately with sambol, dhal or curry.
sources: Sri Lanka Tourism — Food: hoppers as a Sri Lankan staple

name: Indonesian Soto Ayam
imageCredit: Photo: Sakurai Midori, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.1 Japan
summary: Indonesian soto ayam with turmeric-yellow chicken broth, glass noodles, cabbage, sprouts, egg and crisp fried shallots.
lead: Turmeric, ginger and shallots turn chicken broth gold before noodles, cabbage, egg and fried shallots make it a complete bowl.
about: Soto is a large Indonesian family of soups with strong regional differences. Soto ayam means chicken soto, and a broadly familiar form uses a turmeric-yellow chicken broth with aromatics and garnishes such as glass noodles, cabbage, bean sprouts, egg and fried shallots. Some regional versions add coconut milk, potatoes, koya powder or different herbs.
story: Indonesia’s Ministry of Tourism publication Indonesia Spice Up the World calls soto ayam quintessential Indonesian comfort food and highlights chicken, ginger, shallots, turmeric and glass noodles as key components. Treating soto ayam as one rigid national recipe would erase its regional variety, so this page offers an accessible clear-broth yellow version while directing readers to understand it as one doorway into a much larger soup tradition.
caveat: Soto ayam changes substantially across Java and other Indonesian regions. This clear turmeric-broth home adaptation is intentionally generic and does not claim to reproduce a specific Lamongan, Kudus, Medan or other regional soto.
prepNotes: Toast whole aromatics first
Bruised lemongrass and lightly cooked spice paste give a cleaner broth than dumping raw spices into water.
Cook noodles separately
Glass noodles left in the soup absorb broth and turn soft during holding.
Build each bowl to order
Fresh lime, herbs and crisp toppings should stay bright instead of simmering in the pot.
ingredients: 1-inch piece fresh turmeric or 1 tsp ground turmeric
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Fried shallots, cilantro, scallion and lime wedges, for serving
steps: Put chicken, water, lemongrass and lime leaves in a pot. Bring to a gentle simmer, skim foam and cook 25–30 minutes until chicken is tender.
Meanwhile grind shallots, garlic, ginger, turmeric, coriander and pepper into a rough paste.
Heat oil in a skillet and fry the spice paste 5–7 minutes until very fragrant and no longer raw-smelling.
Remove cooked chicken from the broth. Stir the fried spice paste into the pot and simmer 10 minutes.
Shred chicken, discarding bones and skin if desired, and return meat to the broth. Season with salt.
Prepare glass noodles separately according to package directions and drain.
Checkpoint: broth should be golden, aromatic and clear enough to pour freely, with turmeric and ginger present but not muddy or chalky.
Divide noodles, cabbage and sprouts among bowls. Ladle over hot chicken and broth, then add egg, fried shallots, herbs and lime.
sources: Indonesia Ministry of Tourism — Indonesia Spice Up the World, Soto Ayam
Indonesia Ministry of Tourism E-Library — Indonesia Spice Up the World
